THE ANALYST IN THE SERVER ROOM

When the network went down, that just made the day perfect. A corrupted database, a failed authentication token, a malfunction in the climate control system, the security camera stuck on maximum zoom—well, I won't go through the whole sorry list. Suffice it to say that when the network went down, that put the seal on everything, as they say.

It was just one of those days. Everybody gets them. Days when you're lucky if you make it to nightfall with no systems crashed.

But of all times for it to happen! For literally months I'd been building my courage up. And finally, just today, I had made up my mind to do it—to propose a partnership to Sofia. I'd messaged her second thing this morning—right after the database corruption—and arranged to meet at her workstation. "Ten o'clock," she'd said, smiling warmly at me through the video chat. She knew why I wanted to talk to her. And when Sofia said ten o'clock, she meant ten o'clock.

Don't get me wrong. I don't mean that Sofia's a perfectionist or obsessive or anything like that. Far from it. But she does have a fixation on that one subject of punctuality. The result of her job, of course. She was a supply chain coordinator. Automated delivery drones, being robots, were invariably punctual. If a drone didn't return on time, no one waited for it. They simply knew that it had been intercepted by some rival facility and had activated its self-destruct protocol.

Well, of course, after working as a supply chain coordinator for three years, Sofia quite naturally was a bit obsessed. I remember one time, shortly after we'd started dating, when I arrived at her station five minutes late and found her having a panic attack. She thought I'd been killed. She couldn't visualize anything less than that keeping me from arriving at the designated moment. When I told her what actually had happened—I'd lost my access badge—she refused to speak to me for four days.

And then the network went down.

Until then, I'd managed somehow to keep the day's minor disasters from ruining my mood. Even while restoring that horrible database—I couldn't very well abandon it, corrupted or no; it was critical infrastructure and people depended on it—and while hurriedly implementing workarounds for that malfunctioning climate control—one hundred and fifty-three levels of server racks could overheat catastrophically—I kept going over and over my prepared partnership speeches, trying to select the most effective one.

I had a Casual Approach: "Hey, I see there's a nice little co-working space available up on level one seventy-three." And I had a Professional Approach: "Sofia, I believe our skills complement each other perfectly. I think we could build something sustainable together. Will you consider a business partnership with me?" I even had a Straightforward Approach: "Sofia, I'm going to need a partner for this next venture, and I can't think of anyone I would rather work with than you."

Actually, though I wouldn't even have admitted this to Sofia, much less to anyone else, I loved her in more than a professional way. But even if we both had been interested in that kind of relationship (neither of us had ever expressed such interest) I knew that Sofia relished her independence too much to ever consider anything beyond a professional partnership.

So I rehearsed my various approaches, realizing that when the time came I would probably be so tongue-tied I'd be capable of no more than a blurted, "Will you partner with me?" and I struggled with authentication tokens and malfunctioning climate controls, and I managed somehow to leave my workstation at five minutes to ten.

Sofia worked down on the hundred fortieth level, thirteen levels away. It never took more than two or three minutes to get to her station, so I was giving myself plenty of time.

But then the network went down.

I tried to access the transit system, and nothing happened. I couldn't understand it.

The automated transit pods had always arrived before, within thirty seconds of being summoned. This was a local line, with pods that traveled between the hundred thirty-third level and the hundred sixty-seventh level, where it was possible to make connections for either the next local or for the express. So the nearest pod couldn't be more than twenty levels away. And this was a non-rush hour.

I tried again, and then I waited some more. I looked at my watch and it was three minutes to ten. Two minutes, and no pod! If it didn't arrive this instant, this second, I would be late.

It didn't arrive.

I vacillated, not knowing what to do next. Stay, hoping the pod would come after all? Or hurry back to my workstation and message Sofia, to give her advance warning that I would be late?

Ten more seconds, and still no pod. I chose the second alternative, raced back down the corridor, and authenticated my way into my workspace. I tried to message Sofia, and the screen lit up with red letters on black: COMMUNICATIONS OFFLINE.

Of course! The entire network was down. Sofia couldn't receive messages. And she knew what I wanted to say to her, so quite naturally she would be waiting, unable to understand why I hadn't arrived.

Frantic, I dashed from the workspace again, back down the corridor to the transit station, and pressed that blasted call button with all my weight. Even if a pod should arrive right now, I would still be almost a minute late.

No matter. It didn't arrive.

I would have been in a howling rage anyway, but this impossibility piled on top of all the other annoyances and breakdowns of the day was just too much. I went into a frenzy, and kicked the transit station wall three times before I realized I was hurting myself more than I was hurting the wall. I limped back to the workspace, fuming, slammed the door behind me, grabbed the facility directory and looked up the number of the Infrastructure Staff. I tried calling, prepared to register a complaint so loud they'd hear me in sub-basement three.

I got some more letters that spelled: NETWORK UNAVAILABLE.

It took three tries before I got through to a harried-looking female technician. "My name is Lucas!" I bellowed. "Lucas Ramirez! I work on the hundred and fifty-third level! I just tried to summon a transit pod and—"

"The-transit-system-is-offline." She said it very rapidly, as though she were growing very used to saying it.

It only stopped me for a second. "Offline? What do you mean offline? Transit systems don't just go offline!" I told her.

"We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible," she rattled. My bellowing was bouncing off her like packets off a firewall.

I changed tactics. First I inhaled, making a production out of it, giving myself a chance to calm down a bit. And then I asked, as rationally as you could please, "Would you mind terribly telling me why the transit system is offline?"

"I-am-sorry-sir-but-that—"

"Stop," I said. I said it quietly, too, but she stopped. I saw her looking at me. She hadn't done that before, she'd merely gazed blankly at her screen and parroted her responses.

But now she was actually looking at me.

I took advantage of the fact. Calmly, rationally, I said to her, "I would like to tell you something, Miss. I would like to tell you just what you people have done to me by taking the transit system offline. You have ruined my life."

She blinked, open-mouthed. "Ruined your life?"

"Precisely." I found it necessary to inhale again, even more slowly than before. "I was on my way," I explained, "to propose a partnership to a woman whom I deeply respect and admire. In every way but one, she is the perfect partner. Do you understand me?"

She nodded, wide-eyed. I had stumbled on a romantic, though I was too preoccupied to notice it at the time.

"In every way but one," I continued. "She has one small quirk, a fixation about punctuality. And I was supposed to meet her at ten o'clock. I'm late!" I gestured emphatically at the screen. "Do you realize what you've done, taking the transit system offline? Not only won't she partner with me, she won't even speak to me! Not now! Not after this!"

"Sir," she said tremulously, "please don't shout."

"I'm not shouting!"

"Sir, I'm terribly sorry. I understand your—"

"You understand?" I trembled with speechless fury.

She looked all about her, and then leaned closer to the screen. "We're not supposed to give this information out, sir," she said, her voice low, "but I'm going to tell you, so you'll understand why we had to do it. I think it's perfectly awful that it had to ruin things for you this way. But the fact of the matter is—" she leaned even closer to the screen—"there's an intruder in the server room."

It was my turn to be stunned.

I just gaped at her. "A—a what?"

"An intruder. She was discovered on the hundred forty-seventh level, and managed to get into the main server room before Security could catch her. She locked it down from the inside. But Security is doing everything it can think of to get her out."

"Well—but why should there be any problem about getting her out?"

"She has administrative access. We can't control anything from outside at all. And when anyone tries to get into the server room, she threatens to wipe all the data."

That sounded catastrophic. "She threatens to wipe everything?"

"She has root access," the technician explained, "and she's holding the entire system hostage."

"Oh," I said. "So it might take a while."

She leaned so close this time that even I, distracted as I was, took note of her concerned expression. She whispered, "They're afraid they'll have to negotiate with her."

"Oh, no!"

She nodded solemnly. "I'm terribly sorry, sir," she said. Then she glanced to her right, suddenly straightened up again, and said, "We-will-resume-service-as-soon-as-possible." Click. Blank screen.

For a minute or two, all I could do was sit and absorb what I'd been told. An intruder in the server room! An intruder who had managed to work her way all the way up to the hundred forty-seventh level before being detected!

What in the world was the matter with Security? If things were getting that lax, the Facility was doomed, encryption or no. Who knew how many more intruders there were in the Facility, still undetected?

I paused, realizing with some surprise that this was the first time I'd thought about Security in... I couldn't actually remember how long. Months? Years? The Facility, after all, was self-sufficient and completely secure. No one ever left, no one ever entered. Within our walls, we were a community, two hundred levels high. Most drones returned on schedule; occasionally one didn't. Occasionally there were Security alerts that scrolled across our screens during work hours, which most of us minimized to focus on more pressing tasks. Occasionally agents of our own left the Facility in tiny shielded vehicles, though I couldn't recall the last time anyone had mentioned this happening.

Dr. Morrison—Advanced Facility History, when I was fifteen years old—had private names for every major conflict of the twenty-first century. There was the First Cyber War, the Second Cyber War, and the Great Network Collapse, known to the textbooks of course as the Information Wars.

The rise of the Facilities, according to Dr. Morrison, was the result of many many factors, but two of the most important were the population concentration and the Geneva Protocols. The population concentration, of course, meant that there were continuously more and more people but never any more space. So that housing, in the historically short time of one century, made a complete transformation from horizontal expansion to vertical. Before 2000, the vast majority of human beings lived in structures of from one to five stories. By 2100, everybody lived in Facilities.

And the Geneva Protocols.

It seems there was a power-struggle between two sets of then-existing nations (they were something like Facilities, only horizontal instead of vertical) and both sets were equipped with cyber weapons. The Geneva Protocols began by stating that infrastructure warfare was unthinkable, and added that just in case anyone happened to think of it only tactical cyber weapons could be used. After the war almost the whole network infrastructure was quite dangerously compromised. Except for the Facilities—or at least those of them which had in time installed quantum encryption.

However, what with all of the other protocols which were broken during the Information Wars, by the time it was finished nobody was quite sure any more who was on whose side. That facility over there on the horizon might be an ally. And then again it might not.

But now there was an intruder in the server room.

I sat shaken, digesting this news, until suddenly I remembered Sofia.

I leaped to my feet, reading from my watch that it was now ten-fifteen. I dashed once more from the workspace and down the corridor to the transit station, praying that the intruder had been captured by now.

The system was still down.

I sagged against the wall, thinking dismal thoughts. Then I noticed the door to the right of the transit station. Through that door were the maintenance stairs.

I hadn't paid any attention to it before. No one ever uses the stairs except adventurous young technicians playing capture-the-flag. I myself hadn't set foot on a flight of stairs since I was twelve years old.

Well, according to Dr. Morrison (a walking database of unnecessary information), the Facility had been built when there still had been such things as building codes, anachronistic even then, which required emergency stairs in every structure constructed.

And now, after all these years, the stairs might prove useful after all. It was only thirteen flights to Sofia's level.

The door opened reluctantly. Who knew how many years it had been since last this door had been opened? It squeaked and groaned and finally opened halfway. I stepped through to the dusty landing, took a deep breath, and started down. Eight steps and a landing, eight steps and a level.

On the landing between one fifty and one forty-nine, there was a small door. I paused, looking curiously at it, and saw that at one time letters had been stenciled on it. The letters had long since faded, but they left a lighter residue of dust than that which covered the rest of the door. And so the words could still be read, if with difficulty.

They said:

EMERGENCY ACCESS
SERVER ROOM
AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL
ONLY
KEEP LOCKED

I frowned, wondering immediately why this door wasn't being firmly guarded by at least a squad of Security personnel.

As I stood there, pondering these possibilities, the door opened and the intruder came out, holding a device that looked like it could cause serious harm.

She couldn't have been anyone else but the intruder. The device, in the first place. The fact that she looked harried and upset and terribly nervous, in the second place. And, of course, the fact that she came from the server room.

Looking back, I think she must have been just as startled as I when we came face to face like that. We formed a brief tableau, both of us open-mouthed and wide-eyed.

Unfortunately, she recovered first.

She closed the emergency door behind her, quickly but quietly. Her device stopped waving around and instead pointed directly at my middle. "Don't move!" she whispered harshly. "Don't make a sound!"

I did exactly as I was told. Which left me quite free to study her.

She was rather tall, perhaps three inches taller than me, with sharp features and intense eyes. She wore dark clothing, practical for moving unseen. She looked exactly like an intruder... which is to say that she didn't look like an intruder, she looked remarkably ordinary.

Her gaze darted this way and that. Then she gestured with her free hand at the descending stairs and whispered, "Where do they go?"

I had to clear my throat before I could speak. "All the way down," I said.

"Good," she said—just as we both heard a sudden raucous squealing from perhaps four flights down, a squealing which could be nothing but the opening of a corridor door. It was followed by the heavy thud of ascending boots. Security!

But if I had any visions of imminent rescue, the intruder dashed them. She said, "Where do you work?"

"One fifty-three," I said. This was a desperate and dangerous woman. I knew my only slim chance of safety lay in answering her questions promptly, cooperating with her until and unless I saw a chance to either escape or capture her.

"All right," she whispered. "Go on." She prodded me with the device.

And so we went back up the stairs to one fifty-three, and stopped at the door. She stood close behind me, the device pressed against my back, and grated in my ear, "I'll have this device in my pocket. If you make one false move I'll use it. Now, we're going to your workspace. We're colleagues, just walking along together. You got that?"

I nodded.

"All right. Let's go."

We went. I have never in my life seen that long corridor quite so empty as it was right then. No one came out of any of the workspaces, no one emerged from any of the branch corridors. We walked to my workspace. I authenticated the door and we went inside.

Once the door was closed behind us, she visibly relaxed, sagging against the door, her device hand hanging limp at her side, a nervous smile playing across her lips.

I looked at her, judging the distance between us, wondering if I could leap at her before she could bring the device up again. But she must have read my intentions on my face. She straightened, shaking her head. She said, "Don't try it. I don't want to hurt you. I don't want to hurt anybody, but I will if I have to. We'll just wait here together until the search passes us. Then I'll secure you, so you won't be able to alert Security too soon, and I'll leave. If you don't try any silly heroics, nothing will happen to you."

"You'll never get away," I told her. "The whole Facility is on alert."

"You let me worry about that," she said. She licked her lips. "You got any coffee?"

"Yes."

"Make me a cup. And don't get any bright ideas about using it as a weapon."

"I only have my day's allotment," I protested. "Just enough for two cups, morning and afternoon."

"Two cups is fine," she said. "One for each of us."

And now I had yet another grudge against this blasted intruder. Which reminded me again of Sofia. From the looks of things, I wasn't ever going to get to her workspace. By now she was probably mourning our potential partnership.

As I made the coffee, she asked me questions. My name first, and then, "What do you do for a living?"

I thought fast. "I'm a supply chain analyst," I said. That was a lie, of course, but I'd heard enough about supply chain management from Sofia to be able to maintain the fiction should she question me further about it.

Actually, I was a cybersecurity specialist. The subjects I worked on included intrusion detection, threat analysis and penetration testing—talents I would prefer to disclose to her in my own fashion, when the time came.

She was quiet for a moment. "What about the supply drones? Do you ever analyze their data logs?"

I had no idea what she was talking about, and admitted as much.

"When they come back," she said. "What kind of data do they collect about conditions outside? Don't you people ever review them?"

"Of course not," I told her. I was on secure ground now, with Sofia's information to guide me. "All data is sanitized and verified before it's integrated into our systems."

"I know that," she said impatiently. "But don't you ever analyze the raw data before sanitizing it?"

"No. Why should we?"

"To find out what conditions are actually like outside."

"For what? Who cares about that?"

She studied me for a long moment. "When was the last time you thought about what's outside these walls?"

The question caught me off guard. I opened my mouth to answer, then closed it again. When had I last thought about it? I couldn't remember. The supply drones went out and came back. Security handled... whatever Security handled. I had my databases to maintain, my climate controls to monitor, my partnership proposal to rehearse.

"I'm very busy," I said finally. "I have important work."

"I'm sure you do." She took the coffee I offered. "And I'm sure Security is busy too. Very busy keeping everyone safe from threats that require constant vigilance." She sipped. "Tell me, when was the last Security briefing you attended?"

"We receive alerts," I said defensively. "They scroll across our screens."

"And do you read them?"

I thought of the orange banners I routinely minimized. "The relevant ones."

"How do you know which ones are relevant if you don't read them?"

I didn't have an answer for that.

She set down her coffee and leaned toward me, her eyes gleaming with intensity. "Don't you ever wish to go Outside?"

Incredible! I nearly spilled boiling coffee all over myself. "Outside? Of course not!"

"Why not?"

"Because it's—" I stopped. Because it's what? Dangerous? How did I know that? When had I last seen any evidence of danger? "Because we're safe here," I finished lamely.

"Safe from what, exactly?"

"From... the other facilities. From whatever's out there."

"Have you ever seen what's out there?"

"No, but—"

"Has anyone you know ever seen it?"

"The agents—"

"When did you last speak to an agent? When did you last see a report from one?"

I fell silent. The truth was, I had never spoken to an agent. I had never seen a report. I had simply assumed they existed, that they went out and came back with vital intelligence that Security used to keep us safe.

She must have read something in my expression, because she nodded slowly. "That's what I thought."

"Listen, you," she said, her voice dropping. "I come from a Facility about eighty miles north of here. I came here on foot, without any sort of protective equipment at all."

I stared at her. "That's impossible."

"Is it? Have you tested the air quality outside recently? Have you checked radiation levels? Have you done any environmental monitoring at all?"

"That's not my department."

"Whose department is it?"

I didn't know. I realized, with a strange sinking feeling, that I had no idea who was responsible for monitoring external conditions. I had simply assumed someone was doing it. Somewhere. In some department I'd never visited.

"I'm a trained environmental scientist," she went on. "In my facility, I worked on air quality monitoring. Theoretically, I believed that there was a chance the environment Outside was recovering by now. But I wanted to test the theory through field research, and the Council wouldn't let me."

"Of course they wouldn't," I said. "It's too dangerous."

"According to whom?"

"According to..." I trailed off.

"So I left. I walked out. And I've been traveling from Facility to Facility." She paused. "Do you know what I've found? The same thing everywhere. The same routines. The same assumptions. The same people who've built comfortable lives and don't particularly want them disrupted."

"That's absurd," I protested. "We're vigilant. We maintain constant awareness of external threats."

"Really? Name one."

"I—the other facilities—"

"Which other facilities? What are their names? Where are they located? What specific threats do they pose?"

I couldn't answer. I realized I had never known these things. They had simply been... there. Abstract dangers that justified our walls, our protocols, our way of life.

"Your facility sends out agents, too, doesn't it?" she demanded.

"Well, of course."

"And what are they supposed to do?"

"Well—" It was such a pointless question, it seemed silly to even answer it. "They're supposed to look for indications of an attack by one of the other facilities."

"And do they find any indications, ever?"

"I'm sure I don't know," I told her coldly. "That would be classified information."

"Classified." She laughed bitterly. "How convenient. The evidence is always classified, always handled by someone else, always just beyond your reach. And you never think to ask why."

"Security handles those matters," I said stiffly. "That's their job."

"And your job is to maintain databases and fix climate controls and propose partnerships to punctual women. And never, ever ask uncomfortable questions."

"I ask questions all the time! I'm a cybersecurity specialist!" The words were out before I could stop them.

She raised an eyebrow. "I thought you were a supply chain analyst."

I felt my face redden. "I lied. Obviously. You're an intruder."

"Obviously." She smiled grimly. "A cybersecurity specialist. Tell me, in your professional capacity, when was the last time you detected an actual intrusion attempt? Not a drill. Not a simulation. A real attack from an external source."

I thought about it. I had been working in cybersecurity for seven years. I had run countless drills, analyzed innumerable simulations, written extensive reports on theoretical vulnerabilities. But an actual attack?

"The systems are secure," I said. "That's why there are no attacks."

"Or maybe there are no attacks because there's no one attacking." She set down her coffee cup. "Maybe every facility is huddled behind its walls, convinced that every other facility is planning an assault, and none of them ever are."

"You can't know that."

"Neither can you. That's my point." She began pacing the room. "You're a cybersecurity specialist who's never detected a real intrusion. You work in a facility that sends out agents whose reports you've never seen. You're protected by a Security department whose briefings you don't read. And you're absolutely certain that everything outside these walls is deadly and dangerous."

"Because it is," I insisted. "The Information Wars—"

"Were how long ago? Fifty years? Sixty? And you're still living like it's yesterday." She stopped pacing and faced me directly. "Ecosystems recover. Radiation dissipates. Even the worst environmental damage doesn't last forever. But fear? Fear can last generations. Fear can become tradition. Fear can become so comfortable that people stop even recognizing it as fear."

Before I could respond, we both heard a sound outside my door. Heavy footsteps. Multiple people.

Security had found us.

The woman looked at me one last time. "Ask Sofia about the drone data logs sometime. The raw data, before it's sanitized. Ask her what's in them—if she even knows."

Then she moved with surprising speed, securing me to my chair with some kind of quick-release restraint, and disappeared through a maintenance hatch I hadn't even known existed in my own workspace.

By the time Security broke through my door, she was gone.

The Security team was efficient and thorough. They searched my workspace, documented the restraints, took my statement. They were particularly interested in what the intruder had said to me.

"Standard disinformation tactics," the team leader assured me. "They try to plant seeds of doubt. Make you question your safety. It's psychological warfare, nothing more."

"Of course," I said.

"You did well not engaging with her claims. The best thing is to forget this whole conversation."

"Of course," I said again.

They left. I sat in my workspace, staring at my restored database, my repaired climate controls, my functional authentication systems. Everything was back to normal. The network was up. The transit pods were running. Life could resume.

I pulled up my calendar and saw that I had missed my meeting with Sofia by six hours.

Three days later, I finally made it to Sofia's workspace. She was surprised to see me, having heard about my encounter with the intruder.

"Are you all right?" she asked. "That must have been terrifying."

"It was... interesting," I said. Then, before I could stop myself: "Sofia, in your work with the supply drones—do you ever look at their raw sensor data? Before it's processed?"

She looked confused. "Why would I? The processed data tells us everything we need to know about delivery schedules and route efficiency."

"But the raw data—environmental readings, atmospheric conditions—"

"That's not my department," she said. "Someone else handles that, I assume. Why?"

I looked at her. She was brilliant, competent, the best supply chain coordinator in the facility. She managed hundreds of drones, coordinated thousands of deliveries, maintained the lifeblood of our entire community. And she had never once wondered what those drones saw when they flew outside our walls.

Neither had I.

"No reason," I said. "Just curious."

She smiled. "So. About that partnership proposal?"

I took a deep breath. "Actually, I was thinking we might work on a different kind of project first. Something involving data analysis. Historical records. Supply drone sensor logs."

"That sounds boring," she said. "What would we even be looking for?"

I thought of the intruder's questions. Of Security's efficient dismissal. Of all the things I had never thought to ask in my entire life.

"I'm not sure yet," I admitted. "But I think it might be important."

Sofia studied me for a long moment. Then she nodded slowly.

"All right," she said. "Show me what you're thinking."

I pulled up my workstation and started searching for records I'd never thought to look for before.

It would take us weeks to find anything useful. The data was scattered across systems, classified under obscure protocols, buried in archives that no one had accessed in years. Most of what we found was routine and unremarkable.

But occasionally—just occasionally—we found something that made us pause. A sensor reading that didn't match our assumptions. A log entry that raised more questions than it answered. A gap in the records where data should have been.

We never found proof of anything. We never confirmed the intruder's claims. We never discovered whether the world outside was safe or deadly, recovering or ruined.

But we started asking questions.

And sometimes, that's where everything begins.
problem_data.question: How did living in a state of isolation affect the facility inhabitants?
problem_data.correct_answer: They lived full lives with external dangers merely lurking at the backs of their minds, accepting isolation as normal without questioning its continued necessity.
problem_data.incorrect_answer: They maintained constant awareness of external threats and regularly questioned whether isolation was still necessary.
